e.t: Abisak, also rendered Avisak, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies the same named person throughout its five occurrences in the Greek Old Testament, all in 1 Kings. The name appears in 1 Kings 1:3, 1:15, 2:17, 2:21, and 2:22. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic function is simply to name Abisak, a person mentioned in that account.

This adjective describes someone or something as “inglorious” or “disreputable”—lacking honor, esteem, or a good name. It points to a condition viewed negatively by others, whether because of shameful conduct, low standing, or a damaged reputation. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Sirach and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described.

Aigla, also given as Egla, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a woman in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in 2 Samuel 3:5. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identity but does not provide additional meaning about the person or the event.

This adjective describes someone who is blameless—without a charge of wrongdoing standing against them. It can describe a person’s character or conduct, presenting them as free from blame rather than marked by guilt. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the word occurs 14 times, especially in Proverbs and Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun refers to following or to a train—a sequence or procession that comes along behind or after something. Its basic idea is ordered succession rather than an isolated object. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 1:21, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s core meaning remains a following movement or an accompanying train.

Akrabattēnē, also rendered Akravattini, is a proper name. It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 5:3. Because the available wording gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise local reference cannot be explained further here. The central meaning is therefore the identity of the named entity itself: Akrabattēnē or Akravattini.

This noun means “estrangement”: a condition in which people or parties are no longer close, united, or in normal fellowship. It describes relational separation rather than a physical place or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs two times, in Nehemiah and Jeremiah, so it is an uncommon word within this corpus. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a broken or distant relationship.

This is a proper name, rendered “Ambram” or “Amvram” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs ten times in the LXX corpus, across nine verses, with occurrences in Exodus and 1 Chronicles. Since no verse text is available here, the precise referent and role of the name must be determined from the surrounding genealogy or narrative in each passage.

Ammanitis is a proper name, rendered “Ammanitis.” It functions as a designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times, from 1 Kings through 2 Maccabees. Its precise referent is not identified by the lexical definition alone, so the surrounding passage is needed to determine what or whom it names in each occurrence.

This noun refers to lying down or leaning back—the posture of reclining or resting. Its central idea is a person or body positioned in a lowered, supported way rather than standing or sitting upright. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Song of Songs 1:12. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine the particular force of that reference, but the word itself describes the act or position of lying or leaning back.

This Greek LXX verb means “rear up into manhood,” describing the development of someone toward mature manhood. It presents becoming grown or manly rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Job, at Job 27:14 and Job 33:25. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is growth into adult strength or maturity.

This adjective describes someone or something as “without name; nameless.” It identifies a person or thing whose name is not given or known, rather than describing a particular action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 14:27. The word’s basic meaning remains focused on the absence of a name; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain why the person or thing is unnamed in that passage.

This noun means “registration”: the formal recording or enrollment of people or things. It identifies an act or record rather than describing a person, place, or action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times—once in Daniel and five times in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on what is being registered and how the surrounding sentence uses the term.

This verb means to perplex: to leave someone puzzled, confused, or unsure how to respond. It describes a troubled lack of understanding or direction rather than simply not knowing a fact. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears 18 times, so it can describe this condition in varied situations. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This verb means to depart or part—to move away or become separate. It describes the action of separating rather than a person, place, or object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel, so its broader range of use is not displayed across many passages. Its precise force in that verse must be understood from the surrounding wording and context.

This noun means “wineskin” or “skin,” referring to a container or covering made from animal hide. Its basic sense is a prepared skin used in ordinary life, especially for holding liquid. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times across 14 verses, showing that the word belongs to familiar descriptions of skins and leather containers rather than naming an abstract idea. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Atil is a proper name, identifying a person or family in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It occurs once, in Ezra 2:57, and is rendered “Atil.” Because the available wording gives only the name and not the surrounding verse text, its exact identity and role cannot be explained further here. The word functions as a name rather than as a description, action, or quality.

e.h: A Pronoun for He or Him
e.t: This word means “he” or “him,” referring to a male person already identified or understood in the sentence. It is a pronoun, so it stands in place of a person’s name or description rather than naming someone by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it is very common, occurring 14,651 times from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its exact English rendering depends on its place in the sentence, but its central function remains pointing to a male person.

Achimaas, also rendered Akhimaas, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies someone by name in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper noun. The name occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX, across four Old Testament books, with most occurrences in 2 Samuel. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage, but the word itself primarily serves as a person’s name.

Βανηελαμ is a proper name, rendered as “Banēelam; Vanielam.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:35. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain anything more about the person or the name’s role in that passage.

Basemmath, also rendered Vasemmath, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person in genealogical and family records. It occurs seven times across seven verses, appearing six times in Genesis and once in 1 Kings. The name’s precise significance cannot be determined from the name alone, but its grammatical function is clear: it serves as a proper name for an individual.

Benamioud is a proper personal name, also rendered Venamiuth. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and is not presented here as a descriptive word with a broader abstract meaning. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 34:28. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the lexical evidence identifies it simply as the person’s name.

This word means “in-law,” referring to someone connected to another person through marriage rather than by direct birth. It can describe a relationship such as a son-in-law, daughter-in-law, or another member of a spouse’s family, with the exact relationship determined by the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 26 times, showing that it is a recurring term for family ties formed through marriage.

Gedōr, also rendered Yethor, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named place or person in the genealogical and historical records of Chronicles. It occurs five times, all in five verses: three times in 1 Chronicles and twice in 2 Chronicles. The precise referent depends on the surrounding passage, but the name itself functions as a designation, not as a general theological term.

This noun refers to “sweet wine,” a wine characterized by its sweetness. It names a beverage rather than an action, person, or quality in the abstract. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 32:19, so its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic sense remains clear: it identifies wine that is sweet or richly pleasant in taste.

Dan is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament’s rendering of the Hebrew Scriptures. It identifies the named entity called Dan, rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The word appears 75 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, across 69 verses, and is rendered “Dan” in the available translation evidence. Its precise referent—such as a person, group, or place—must be recognized from the surrounding passage.

This noun means “intimidation” or “timidity”—a fearful shrinking back that weakens a person’s courage. It describes an inward condition of being easily frightened or hesitant rather than standing firmly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs six times, including passages in Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is fearfulness that makes someone vulnerable to discouragement or reluctant action.

This word is an adverb or interjection expressing “come on” or directing attention to “this point.” It serves as a brief spoken call, urging someone forward or focusing attention in the immediate situation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 69 times, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Judges, and 1 Samuel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its normal function is a direct summons or indication.

This verb means “give out”: to distribute, hand over, or make something available to others. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so the surrounding sentence determines what is being given and to whom. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs ten times, including uses in Genesis, Joshua, and Sirach. Its central idea remains the act of passing something along or providing it to others.

This Greek LXX verb means “pluck; pull out the hair.” It describes the physical act of removing hair by pulling it out, rather than merely touching or cutting it. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Job 16:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this entry explains the word’s normal meaning and function, not the particular force it carries in that verse. Its direct sense remains an action of plucking or pulling hair out.

“Glorious” describes something characterized by glory and worthy of praise. As an adjective, it adds this quality to a person, thing, or action rather than naming the quality itself. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:35. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. It is therefore a word of praise, describing something as distinguished by glory.

This verb means to pride oneself on something or to boast loudly. It describes openly claiming honor, greatness, or advantage for oneself rather than merely mentioning a fact. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Psalms, so its normal emphasis is confident self-exaltation expressed in speech. The exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding words, but the central idea remains loud or self-regarding boasting.

This Greek LXX noun means “idol”: an object or image regarded as a deity or used in false worship. It names something treated as a rival to the true God rather than God himself. The word occurs 88 times in the LXX corpus, including the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, so it commonly identifies idols as a recurring biblical subject. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb describes being “at peace”—living or remaining in a condition of peace and calm. It expresses peace as a state rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 18 times in the LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the condition of being at peace.

This Greek LXX verb means “radiant.” It describes something shining with visible brightness or possessing a radiant appearance. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, across two Old Testament passages and four passages in Sirach. Its uses include descriptions associated with light, heavenly glory, and splendor, though the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence. The central idea remains clear: something is radiant, shining forth in brightness.

This Greek LXX verb means “vomit”: to bring the contents of the stomach up through the mouth. It describes a physical bodily action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 31:21. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the verse text is not included here.

This verb means “nod to”: it describes communicating by a movement of the head rather than by spoken words. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Proverbs, so its basic sense is clear. The action describes a silent signal or gesture, expressing communication through a nod. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means to wake out of something or to awake from it. It describes the act of coming out of sleep or another state of unconsciousness, rather than simply being awake. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 5:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is movement from sleep or unawareness into wakefulness.

This verb means “follow after,” describing movement or conduct that comes behind someone or something. It can refer to physically following, but it may also describe pursuing or going after a person, practice, or influence. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 15 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures. Its basic sense remains straightforward: to come after, follow, or pursue rather than lead or go before.

This verb means to “rejoice at” something, expressing gladness directed toward a person, event, or circumstance. It describes an active response rather than a general condition of happiness. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Wisdom 18:6. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its basic sense is taking pleasure or delight in what is being considered.

e.h: To Name or Give a Name
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “named”: it describes giving a person, place, or thing a name. It focuses on the act of assigning or declaring a name, rather than merely mentioning someone who already has one. The word occurs 36 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, from Genesis through 2 Chronicles, showing that naming is a recurring biblical action. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains the act of naming.

Esdras is a personal name, also rendered Ezthras. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 20 times, all within the Old Testament corpus, appearing in Ezra and Nehemiah. It is found nine times in Ezra and eleven times in Nehemiah, with occurrences extending from Ezra 7:1 to Nehemiah 12:36. Its precise significance in any verse comes from the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This adverb means “boldly,” describing speech or action carried out with courage and confidence rather than hesitation or fear. It tells how something is done, not who is acting or what object is involved. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:10. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a courageous, confident manner of acting or speaking.

This Greek LXX noun means “caution” or “prudence”: careful, sensible judgment that helps a person avoid rash action. It describes thoughtful restraint and sound decision-making rather than fear or hesitation. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains wise care in how one thinks or acts.

This noun refers to a hedgehog, also described by the gloss “urchin.” It names a small, spiny animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Isaiah and Zephaniah. The passages associate the animal with places named in prophetic descriptions, but the precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here. The word itself carries a straightforward animal meaning rather than naming a person, action, or abstract idea.

Zathoua, also rendered Zathua, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah. Because no further meaning or name explanation is provided, its significance here is its role as a personal designation, not a translatable concept. English readers may see the spelling “Zathua” in one occurrence, while “Zathoua” preserves another form of the same name.

This verb means “capture”: to seize and take a person or people into custody. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, in passages connected with taking people alive during conflict or preserving them from destruction. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains taking someone captive.

Thachchia, also rendered Thakhkhia, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:62. Because it is a name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of a particular person in the biblical record; the name itself does not provide enough information to explain that person’s character, role, or significance without the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “sacrifice”: an offering presented to God. It names the sacrificial offering itself rather than the act of offering or the person who offers it. The word occurs 15 times across 14 Old Testament verses in the Greek translation, appearing from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its uses include offerings connected with worship, covenant observance, appointed portions, and feasting, though the precise sense in any verse depends on its surrounding passage. The central idea remains an offered sacrifice brought before God.

Thōla, also rendered “Thola,” is a proper personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies people in genealogical and historical records. The name occurs six times in five verses, from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance as a personal name is not explained by the available lexical information; its role is to name a person.

Ial is a proper name—a personal or place name used to identify someone or something rather than describe an action or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 3:7. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not identify whether Ial refers to a person or place. Its precise significance therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Igabes is a proper name, rendered as “Igabēs” or “Igavis.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times, all within two verses in 1 Chronicles 4:9–10. The name itself does not provide a translated meaning beyond identifying the individual, so understanding the person associated with it requires the surrounding passage. Its occurrence is limited to this brief genealogical setting.

Idoud, also rendered Ithuth, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 23:19. Because the available verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s family connection or role in that passage cannot be stated safely. Its basic meaning is therefore its identity as a proper name.

This word is a proper name: “Iechemias” or “Iekhemias.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 2:41. The available meaning is limited to the personal name itself, so its significance as a name in that genealogy must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the word alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “desire”: it expresses wanting or longing for something. As a verb, it describes the act of desiring rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Job 3:21. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of that occurrence, but the word’s basic meaning remains the expression of desire.

Istōb, also rendered Istov, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Greek text, both times in 2 Samuel 10, at 10:6 and 10:8. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be identified more closely here; however, its function is clearly that of a proper name preserved as Istob in English rendering.

This word means “just as” or “like,” marking a comparison or showing that one statement corresponds to another. It can connect ideas by indicating similarity, resemblance, or the manner in which something happens. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 242 times, so it serves as a broadly used linking word rather than naming a person, object, or action. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the statements it connects.

This noun means “division into parts,” describing the separating or apportioning of something into distinct portions. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 13:14, so its normal sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word points to an arrangement in which something is distributed by parts rather than treated as one undivided whole.

This Greek LXX verb means “rejoice”: to express gladness or delight. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it tells what someone does when responding with joy. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Zephaniah 3:14. Its basic meaning is clear from the direct definition and does not require adding a more specific emotional or spiritual idea without the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “hollow” or “hollow out.” It describes making something hollow, or expressing the condition of being hollow. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Jeremiah: Jeremiah 14:2 and Jeremiah 15:9. These occurrences belong to the Old Testament Greek corpus, and the word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic idea remains the removal of what fills or supports the inside, leaving something hollow.

This word means “cinnamon,” the name of a spice. It is a noun used for the substance itself, rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs five times, appearing in Exodus, Proverbs, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the spice cinnamon.

This Greek LXX word is a proper name, given as “Koilē; Kili.” It functions as a name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. Its exact referent must be determined from the surrounding verse, since the lexical information identifies the name but does not provide the verse text. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Leviticus and 1–2 Maccabees.

This verb means “obtain,” describing the act of coming into possession of something. It functions as an action word, not as the name of a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, it occurs 20 times, showing use across multiple passages rather than only one setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being obtained and the surrounding sentence. It appears in texts ranging from Genesis through 4 Maccabees.

This adverb means “imperceptibly”: in a way that is not noticed or detected. It describes an action or change taking place without attracting attention, so readers understand that something happened quietly or beyond ordinary awareness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the same: something occurs without being perceived.

This Greek LXX noun means “mane,” the longer hair growing around an animal’s neck. It names a visible physical feature rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek text of Joshua, in Joshua 15:2, Joshua 15:5, and Joshua 18:19. Since those passages are boundary descriptions and the verse text is not included here, the word’s basic meaning is clear, while its exact reference in each description belongs to the surrounding passage.

This word means “in a blessed way” or “blessed.” As an adverb, it describes how something is done or how someone is regarded, marking a condition of blessing or happiness rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears once, in 4 Maccabees 12:1. The exact force of that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Machō, also rendered Makho, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 16:7. The available information identifies it as a proper name, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain whom it names or what role that person has in the passage. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the context of Joshua 16:7 rather than to a broader lexical meaning. This word means “neither of the two.” It is an adjective used to describe two alternatives when both are excluded. In other words, it points to neither one option nor the other, rather than choosing between them. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Proverbs 24:21. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a clear denial of both possibilities. This word should be kept distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary because this entry belongs to the Greek Old Testament corpus.

This word means “hired,” describing a person who works for pay or something connected with being hired. It can function as an adjective or as a noun referring to a hired person. In the LXX corpus, it occurs five times, in Leviticus, Job, and Sirach, showing its use across passages concerned with ordinary human work and service. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains someone or something associated with being hired.

Naged, also rendered Nayeth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 5:16. The available lexical information establishes the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

Noom is a personal name, rendered as “Noom.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:15. Because the available passage text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that verse cannot be described further. Its ordinary lexical function is simply to designate the person called Noom.

This noun refers to a “gadfly,” also called a “breese”—a flying insect known for harassing or stinging. It names the creature itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees, at 2:3 and 3:17. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the image functions in either passage; the word’s basic meaning remains the insect named by the gloss.

This noun refers to “divination by the flight,” meaning an attempt to discover guidance or hidden knowledge by interpreting how something flies. It names a form of divination rather than ordinary observation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in 1 Samuel and Jeremiah, so its meaning is consistent but its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to a kind of grain, specifically spelt. It is a noun naming a cultivated cereal used among other grains. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Ezekiel, so its meaning is specific rather than a broad term for food or agriculture. The word identifies the grain itself; the surrounding verse determines how that grain functions in the passage. It should therefore be understood as the name of a particular grain variety.

This Greek LXX adverb means “by no means.” It expresses a strong denial or rejection, indicating that something is not to be accepted or understood under any circumstance. As an adverb, it modifies an action, statement, or idea by emphatically ruling it out. The word occurs seven times in the deuterocanonical books of the LXX corpus, especially in 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular sentence comes from the surrounding context.

This word means “mob.” It is a verb describing the action of mobbing—people acting together as a crowd rather than as isolated individuals. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, so its normal sense is clear, but its precise force in 3 Maccabees 5:41 must be determined from that verse and its surrounding passage. It should be understood as an action word, not a name for a person or object.

This LXX adverb means “all the nation,” expressing something that applies to an entire people collectively rather than only to selected individuals. It describes the scope of an action, condition, or experience as reaching the nation as a whole. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Wisdom 19:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its basic meaning emphasizes complete national scope.

This Greek LXX noun refers to consolation or encouragement—support that comforts and strengthens someone. It describes a message or help given to lift another person, rather than an action of correcting or judging them. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 3:18, so its broader range must be understood from its basic meaning rather than from many examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “incidental.” It describes something that accompanies the main matter without being its central focus. The word therefore points to a related or accompanying circumstance rather than the primary subject itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:19. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains something incidental—present alongside the main matter rather than defining it.

This verb means “try” or “test”—to put someone or something through an experience that reveals what they will do or whether they are genuine. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe testing people, testing faithfulness, or attempting something. It occurs 45 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on who is doing the testing and what is being tested.

This Greek LXX verb means to drink—to take liquid into the body. It describes the ordinary act of drinking and can be used wherever the surrounding passage speaks of consuming a beverage or other liquid. The word occurs 249 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented in this corpus, showing that it is a common action word rather than a specialized term. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “more frequently” or “oftener.” It describes an action or event that happens with greater frequency than another, or happens repeatedly. The word functions by comparing how often something occurs rather than describing the action itself. It appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical writings, including Psalms, Isaiah, Sirach, and Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what action or event the surrounding sentence compares or repeats.

This verb means “enrich”: to make someone or something richer. It describes an action that adds to another’s wealth or abundance, rather than simply describing possession.
